blocks.text: A car's front crumple zone and a valve spring both store or absorb energy in the metal, but one must give the energy back unchanged and the other must destroy it by permanent deformation. The same stress-strain curve tells you which metal suits which job.

blocks.markdown: The area under a stress-strain curve has units of stress times strain, which is N/m$^2$ = J/m$^3$: **energy per unit volume**. Take a small element of material, load it, and the area up to a given strain is the strain energy absorbed per unit volume. Two special areas matter in design: the elastic area up to yield, called resilience, and the total area to fracture, called toughness.

blocks.title: Modulus of resilience and toughness
blocks.text: The modulus of resilience $U_r$ is the strain energy per unit volume absorbed up to the yield point and recovered on unloading. The toughness $U_t$ is the strain energy per unit volume absorbed up to fracture, which is the whole area under the stress-strain curve. Both are in J/m$^3$ (1 MJ/m$^3$ = 1 MPa $\times$ strain 1).

blocks.caption: Linear elastic region only: $\sigma=E\varepsilon$. $\sigma_y$ is the yield strength (Pa), $E$ the Young's modulus (Pa).

blocks.title: Modulus of resilience of a structural steel
blocks.prompt: A structural steel has a yield strength $\sigma_y=350$ MPa and a typical Young's modulus $E=205$ GPa. Find its modulus of resilience and the energy stored in a 2.0 litre volume stressed uniformly to yield.

steps.text: Evaluate $U_r=\sigma_y^2/(2E)$ with consistent units (MPa for both).

blocks.answer: $U_r=0.299$ MJ/m$^3$, so about 0.6 kJ is stored in 2 litres and is fully recoverable.

blocks.markdown: **Toughness.** The plastic part of the curve is not a straight line, so toughness is found by integrating the measured curve, for example with the trapezium rule, or estimated from a simple model. For a ductile metal the curve rises to the ultimate strength $\sigma_u$ at large strain, so the area is roughly the average of $\sigma_y$ and $\sigma_u$ multiplied by the fracture strain $\varepsilon_f$. For a brittle material the curve is nearly linear to fracture, and the area is roughly a triangle.

blocks.caption: Approximations from the shape of the engineering curve; $\varepsilon_f$ is the strain at fracture and $\sigma_f$ the fracture stress.

blocks.title: Estimating toughness of a ductile alloy
blocks.prompt: A ductile alloy has $\sigma_y=250$ MPa, $\sigma_u=400$ MPa and a strain at fracture $\varepsilon_f=0.30$. Estimate its toughness and compare with its modulus of resilience for $E=70$ GPa.

steps.text: Average of the two strengths: $(250+400)/2=325$ MPa.

blocks.answer: $U_t\approx97.5$ MJ/m$^3$ against $U_r=0.446$ MJ/m$^3$; for ductile metals, the plastic region stores or dissipates over 200 times more energy than the elastic region.

rows: Springs, elastic energy storage, shock-absorbing mounts
Small; ceramics and hardened steels at low ductility
blocks.caption: Approximations from the shape of an engineering stress-strain curve.

items: High yield strength and low modulus maximise resilience: this is why spring materials are strong and relatively compliant.
Large ductility gives large toughness even if yield strength is modest.
Compare two alloys by computing the relevant area from stated stress-strain data, not by comparing a single strength.
The elastic energy is recovered on unloading; the plastic energy is dissipated, mainly as heat.

blocks.title: Check your units
blocks.text: If stresses are in MPa and strain is dimensionless, the area comes out in MJ/m$^3$ directly. Multiplying by a volume in m$^3$ then gives joules after converting MJ to J.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the two
blocks.text: A material with a high UTS is not necessarily tough, and one with a high toughness is not necessarily good for springs. Always match the area to the function.

points: Resilience is the elastic area to yield, $U_r=\sigma_y^2/(2E)$, and toughness is the area to fracture; both are strain-energy densities in J/m$^3$.
Toughness of a ductile metal can be estimated as $\tfrac12(\sigma_y+\sigma_u)\varepsilon_f$.
To compare alloys for energy absorption, compute the area for each using their stress-strain data and select the larger toughness; for energy storage use resilience.

questions.stem: Which is the SI unit of modulus of resilience or toughness, and what is its physical meaning?

options.text: J/m$^3$ (equivalently Pa), energy absorbed per unit volume
J, energy absorbed by the whole specimen

questions.correctOptionText: J/m$^3$ (equivalently Pa), energy absorbed per unit volume

distractorRationale.a: Correct: stress times strain has units of N/m$^2$ x 1 = J/m$^3$.
distractorRationale.b: Neither quantity is a stress gradient.
distractorRationale.c: Energy per volume is a material property; the total energy also depends on the specimen volume.
distractorRationale.d: This is the unit of bond stiffness or surface energy per unit length, not a strain-energy density.

questions.explanation: The area under a stress-strain curve is stress multiplied by dimensionless strain, giving N/m$^2$ = J/m$^3$. It is a strain-energy density, so total energy absorbed is this value multiplied by the volume of material stressed.

questions.stem: A tensile curve is plotted for a steel up to fracture. Which area represents the toughness of the material?

options.text: The whole area under the curve from zero strain to fracture
Only the triangle under the elastic line up to yield
The area above the curve between yield and the UTS
The height of the curve at the UTS

questions.correctOptionText: The whole area under the curve from zero strain to fracture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the total strain energy per unit volume absorbed before fracture.
distractorRationale.b: This is the modulus of resilience.
distractorRationale.c: This is not a defined quantity; energy is absorbed under the curve, not above it.
distractorRationale.d: This is the tensile strength, a stress, not an energy density.

questions.explanation: Toughness here is defined as energy per unit volume absorbed up to fracture, which is the full area under the engineering stress-strain curve. The elastic triangle is only the part that is recovered on unloading.

questions.stem: A material with a very high yield strength must have a high toughness.
questions.explanation: Toughness depends on both strength and ductility, because it is an area under the curve, and a high-strength material that fractures at small strain can enclose little area. For example, a hard but brittle ceramic has a high yield or fracture stress but a small toughness.

questions.stem: An aluminium alloy has a yield strength of 275 MPa and a typical Young's modulus of 70 GPa. Calculate its modulus of resilience in MJ/m$^3$.
questions.explanation: Using $U_r=\sigma_y^2/(2E)$: $U_r=(275)^2/(2\times70000)=75625/140000=0.540$ MPa, which equals 0.540 MJ/m$^3$. Taking stress in MPa and $E$ in MPa gives the result directly in MJ/m$^3$.

questions.stem: A ductile steel has a yield strength of 420 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 560 MPa and a strain at fracture of 0.22. Estimate its toughness in MJ/m$^3$ using the average of the yield and ultimate strengths multiplied by the fracture strain.
questions.explanation: The approximation $U_t\approx\tfrac12(\sigma_y+\sigma_u)\varepsilon_f$ gives $\tfrac12(420+560)\times0.22=490\times0.22=107.8$ MJ/m$^3$. It treats the curve as roughly a trapezoid and is an estimate, not an exact area.

questions.stem: Alloy A has $\sigma_y=300$ MPa, $\sigma_u=450$ MPa and $\varepsilon_f=0.40$. Alloy B has $\sigma_y=900$ MPa, $\sigma_u=1000$ MPa and $\varepsilon_f=0.08$. Using the approximation $U_t\approx\tfrac12(\sigma_y+\sigma_u)\varepsilon_f$ for each, calculate the ratio $U_t(A)/U_t(B)$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: $U_t(A)=\tfrac12(300+450)(0.40)=150$ MJ/m$^3$ and $U_t(B)=\tfrac12(900+1000)(0.08)=76$ MJ/m$^3$. The ratio is $150/76=1.97$, so the weaker but more ductile alloy absorbs about twice as much energy before fracture.

questions.stem: A designer wants a material to absorb the energy of a crash impact by deforming plastically before fracture. Alloy P has $\sigma_y=1100$ MPa, $\sigma_u=1250$ MPa and $\varepsilon_f=0.03$. Alloy Q has $\sigma_y=300$ MPa, $\sigma_u=500$ MPa and $\varepsilon_f=0.25$. Which should be chosen, using $U_t\approx\tfrac12(\sigma_y+\sigma_u)\varepsilon_f$?

options.text: Alloy Q, with about 100 MJ/m$^3$ against about 35 MJ/m$^3$ for P
Alloy P, because its yield and ultimate strengths are higher
Alloy P, because it has the higher modulus of resilience
Neither; the two absorb the same energy

questions.correctOptionText: Alloy Q, with about 100 MJ/m$^3$ against about 35 MJ/m$^3$ for P

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Q's large ductility gives a much bigger area under the curve.
distractorRationale.b: High strength alone does not give a large area; strain at fracture counts equally.
distractorRationale.c: Resilience governs elastic energy storage, not energy absorbed up to fracture.
distractorRationale.d: The estimates are about 35 MJ/m$^3$ for P and 100 MJ/m$^3$ for Q, which differ by nearly a factor of 3.

questions.explanation: For energy absorption in a crash the relevant quantity is toughness, the full area under the curve. $U_t(P)\approx\tfrac12(1100+1250)(0.03)=35$ MJ/m$^3$ and $U_t(Q)\approx\tfrac12(300+500)(0.25)=100$ MJ/m$^3$, so Q is the better choice.

questions.stem: Four candidate spring materials have the following (yield strength in MPa, Young's modulus in GPa): A (500, 200), B (1000, 200), C (1000, 70), D (500, 70). Which stores the most elastic energy per unit volume at yield?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $U_r=\sigma_y^2/2E=7.14$ MJ/m$^3$, the largest of the four.
distractorRationale.b: B has the same yield strength as C but a higher modulus; $U_r=2.50$ MJ/m$^3$.
distractorRationale.c: A has the lowest yield strength of the stiff pair; $U_r=0.625$ MJ/m$^3$.
distractorRationale.d: D has a low modulus but low yield; $U_r=1.79$ MJ/m$^3$, which is less than C.

questions.explanation: The modulus of resilience grows with the square of yield strength and falls with modulus: $U_r=\sigma_y^2/(2E)$. The values are A 0.625, B 2.50, C 7.14 and D 1.79 MJ/m$^3$, so C (high yield, low modulus) is best.

questions.stem: Explain, with reference to areas on an engineering stress-strain curve, the difference between the modulus of resilience and the toughness of a material, and give one application where each is the governing property.
markingGuide: Resilience: area under the elastic (linear) region up to yield, $U_r=\sigma_y^2/(2E)$ (2 marks)
Energy that is recovered on unloading (1 mark)
Toughness: total area to fracture, including plastic region (2 marks)
Application for resilience: a spring or elastic energy store (1 mark)
Application for toughness: crash structure, impact protection or a pressure-vessel steel that must absorb energy before fracture (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Resilience is the triangle under the elastic part of the curve, equal to $\sigma_y^2/(2E)$, and is recovered on unloading. Toughness is the full area to fracture, so ductility matters; springs need resilience while crash members need toughness.

questions.stem: A flexure spring is made either from spring steel ($\sigma_y=1200$ MPa, $E=205$ GPa) or from a titanium alloy ($\sigma_y=1000$ MPa, $E=110$ GPa), both typical values. Calculate the modulus of resilience of each and say which stores more elastic energy per unit volume, and state the assumption.
markingGuide: Titanium stores more per unit volume (1 mark)
Because $U_r$ depends on $\sigma_y^2/E$, a lower modulus can outweigh a lower yield strength (2 marks)
Assumes linear elastic behaviour up to yield and uniform stress state, i.e. uniaxial tension (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Using $U_r=\sigma_y^2/(2E)$ gives 3.51 MJ/m$^3$ for steel and 4.55 MJ/m$^3$ for the titanium alloy. The titanium alloy stores about 30 percent more per unit volume because its modulus is much lower relative to its strength.
